1:2.t: "Injured": the KJV's "sick" and "disease"; the Hebrew covers illness or injury.

Baal-zebub: the name means "lord of the flies". It is probably a mocking change of Baal-zebul, "Baal the prince", a title found in Canaanite texts. By New Testament times Beelzebul had become a name for the prince of demons (Matthew 12:24).

1:4.t: "You will not get up from the bed you are lying on": the KJV's "thou shalt not come down from that bed on which thou art gone up". Beds were often raised, so one "went up" onto them.

1:6.t: "You will not get up from the bed you are lying on": the KJV's "thou shalt not come down from that bed on which thou art gone up". Beds were often raised, so one "went up" onto them.

1:16.t: "You will not get up from the bed you are lying on": the KJV's "thou shalt not come down from that bed on which thou art gone up". Beds were often raised, so one "went up" onto them.

1:8.t: "A hairy man": as in the KJV. The Hebrew may mean a man wearing a garment of hair, the prophet's cloak (compare Zechariah 13:4). "Leather belt around his waist": the KJV's "girdle of leather about his loins".

1:9.t: "Captain of fifty": an officer over a unit of fifty soldiers.

"Man of God" (Hebrew ish ha-elohim): a common title for a prophet in Kings, meaning a man who belongs to God and speaks for Him, not a man who is divine (see 1 Kings 12:22). Elijah's reply plays on the words: ish ("man") and esh ("fire") sound alike in Hebrew, and "man of God" and "fire of God" (1:12) echo each other.

1:17.t: This Jehoram (also spelled Joram) was Ahaziah's brother, a son of Ahab. Another Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, ruled Judah at the same time. 3:1 dates his accession to Jehoshaphat's eighteenth year; the two dates likely reflect a time when Jehoram of Judah reigned alongside his father.

2:3.t: "From over you": the KJV's "from thy head", as a teacher sits above his disciples.

2:5.t: "From over you": the KJV's "from thy head", as a teacher sits above his disciples.

2:12.t: "The chariots of Israel and its horsemen": Elisha (and later King Joash of Elisha himself) calls the prophet Israel's true defense, worth more than its army.

13:14.t: "The chariots of Israel and its horsemen": Elisha (and later King Joash of Elisha himself) calls the prophet Israel's true defense, worth more than its army.

2:16.t: "The Spirit of the LORD": capitalized as the Spirit of God. In verse 15 "the spirit of Elijah" is Elijah's own spirit, so it stays lowercase.

2:23.t: "Baldhead": a taunt, perhaps because Elisha's head was shaved as a prophet or simply bald. "Go on up" mocks Elijah's going up to heaven.

"Young boys" (Hebrew ne'arim qetannim): na'ar can mean anyone from a baby to a young man of military age (it is used of soldiers in 1 Kings 20:14-15). With qetannim ("small") it suggests boys or youths; the KJV's "little children" may make them sound younger than the Hebrew requires. Interpreters differ on their age.

3:2.t: "Sacred pillar": the KJV's "image", a standing stone set up for worship.

3:4.t: "Sheep breeder": the Hebrew noqed is the word used of Amos (Amos 1:1).

3:11.t: "Used to pour water on Elijah's hands": that is, he was Elijah's personal servant.

3:25.t: Kir-hareseth: the KJV spells it Kir-haraseth.

4:23.t: New moons and Sabbaths were days for worship and for visiting a prophet.

4:29.t: "Tuck your cloak into your belt": the KJV's "gird up thy loins", tying up a long robe so as to move fast.

4:39.t: "Wild gourds": probably a bitter, poisonous gourd (colocynth).

4:42.t: Baal-shalishah: the KJV spells it Baal-shalisha.

5:5.t: KJV: "ten talents of silver, and six thousand pieces of gold". The gold unit is not named.

5:12.t: Abana: the Hebrew text reads Amana in some manuscripts.

5:17.t: "As much earth as two mules can carry": Naaman takes soil from the land of Israel so that he can worship the LORD on it back home.

5:24.t: "The hill": the Hebrew ophel, perhaps a hill or citadel in Samaria.

6:5.t: "Oh no": the KJV's "Alas", here and at 6:15.

6:25.t: KJV: "fourscore pieces of silver" (shekels, about 920 grams) and "the fourth part of a cab of dove's dung" (about a third of a liter) for "five pieces of silver" (about 57 grams). "Dove's dung" may be a popular name for a kind of seed pod or wild bulb.

6:32.t: "Son of a murderer": the king was a son of Ahab, who had Naboth killed (1 Kings 21).

7:1.t: KJV: "a measure of fine flour" (a seah, about seven liters) and "two measures of barley" (about fifteen liters) "for a shekel" (about eleven grams of silver), a sudden collapse in prices.

7:16.t: KJV: "a measure of fine flour" (a seah, about seven liters) and "two measures of barley" (about fifteen liters) "for a shekel" (about eleven grams of silver), a sudden collapse in prices.

7:18.t: KJV: "a measure of fine flour" (a seah, about seven liters) and "two measures of barley" (about fifteen liters) "for a shekel" (about eleven grams of silver), a sudden collapse in prices.

7:2.t: "The officer on whose arm the king leaned": the KJV's "a lord on whose hand the king leaned", a chief aide.

7:17.t: "The officer on whose arm the king leaned": the KJV's "a lord on whose hand the king leaned", a chief aide.

7:3.t: Lepers had to live outside the town (Leviticus 13:46).

7:13.t: The servant's point is that the horses will die either way, in the city of hunger or at the hands of the Arameans, so little is lost in sending them.

8:1.t: This visit of the Shunammite woman probably comes before Gehazi's leprosy (5:27), since the stories of Elisha are not told in strict time order.

8:9.t: "Your son": a respectful way for a king to speak of himself to a prophet.

8:10.t: "You will certainly recover": the Hebrew written text reads "you will not recover", but the text as read aloud reads "to him, You will recover", which the KJV follows. Elisha means the illness will not kill Ben-hadad, though he will die.

8:16.t: Jehoram (also spelled Joram) of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, is not the same man as Joram of Israel, son of Ahab. The text uses both spellings for each.

8:19.t: "A lamp": the KJV's "a light", a living descendant on David's throne (1 Kings 11:36).

8:26.t: "Granddaughter": the KJV's "daughter". Athaliah was the daughter of Ahab (8:18) and so the granddaughter of Omri; Hebrew "daughter" covers any female descendant.
compared with 8:25 and 9:29: the twelfth and eleventh years of Joram likely reflect different ways of counting a king's first year.

9:1.t: "Tuck your robe into your belt": the KJV's "gird up thy loins", tying up a long robe so as to move fast (see 4:29). "Flask": the KJV's "box".

9:8.t: "Every male, slave or free": the KJV's "him that pisseth against the wall, and him that is shut up and left in Israel". The first phrase is a blunt idiom for every male, used in threats against a whole family line; the second is a fixed phrase that probably means everyone, whether bound or free. See 1 Kings 14:10.

9:13.t: Spreading cloaks under a man was an act of homage to a new king (compare Matthew 21:8).

9:27.t: "The garden house": the Hebrew may be a place name, Beth-haggan, near Jezreel.

9:30.t: "Painted her eyes": the KJV's "painted her face"; the Hebrew refers to dark eye paint.

9:31.t: Zimri killed his master King Elah and reigned only seven days (1 Kings 16:9-18). Jezebel's question warns Jehu that a murderer of kings will not last.

10:1.t: "Sons": here meaning male descendants, sons and grandsons. "Rulers of Jezreel": some Greek manuscripts read "rulers of the city".

10:12.t: "The shearing house of the shepherds": the Hebrew may be a place name, Beth-eked of the Shepherds.

10:14.t: "The shearing house of the shepherds": the Hebrew may be a place name, Beth-eked of the Shepherds.

10:13.t: "Queen mother": the Hebrew gevirah, the king's mother, who held an honored office at court; here Jezebel.

10:15.t: Jehonadab (Jonadab) the son of Rechab founded the Rechabites, who lived in tents and drank no wine (Jeremiah 35:6-10).

10:22.t: "The man in charge of the wardrobe": the KJV's "him that was over the vestry", the room where ceremonial robes were kept.

10:25.t: "The inner shrine of the temple": the KJV's "the city of the house of Baal". The Hebrew probably means the inner, fortified part of the temple.

10:26.t: "Sacred pillars" and "pillar": the KJV's "images" and "image", standing stones set up for worship (see 3:2).

10:32.t: "Cut away parts of Israel": the KJV's "cut Israel short".

11:2.t: Joash and Jehoash are two spellings of the same name, used for this king and also for Jehoash of Israel (13:10).

11:4.t: "Captains": the Hebrew is Kari, probably the Carites, foreign soldiers in the royal guard, like the Cherethites of David's day.

11:19.t: "Captains": the Hebrew is Kari, probably the Carites, foreign soldiers in the royal guard, like the Cherethites of David's day.

11:6.t: "Hold it secure": the KJV's "that it be not broken down"; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

11:12.t: "The testimony": probably a copy of the covenant law, which the king was to keep (Deuteronomy 17:18-19). "Long live the king": the KJV's "God save the king"; the Hebrew is "May the king live" (see 1 Kings 1:25).

11:14.t: "By the pillar": the king's place in the temple court, perhaps one of the two bronze pillars (1 Kings 7:21).

12:4.t: "The money from the census": the KJV's "the money of every one that passeth the account", the half shekel paid by each person counted (Exodus 30:12-16). "The money each person is assessed": payments for vows (Leviticus 27:2-8).

12:5.t: "From his own contacts": the KJV's "of his acquaintance". The Hebrew may mean donors the priests knew, or the treasurers who handled the funds.

12:7.t: "From his own contacts": the KJV's "of his acquaintance". The Hebrew may mean donors the priests knew, or the treasurers who handled the funds.

12:10.t: "Bagged and counted": the KJV's "put up in bags, and told", where "told" means counted.

12:20.t: "House of Millo": Millo was a terraced fortification in Jerusalem (1 Kings 9:15).

13:5.t: "A deliverer": the text does not say who, perhaps the Assyrian king who weakened Aram, or Jehoash and Jeroboam II (13:25, 14:27).

"Deliverer" (Hebrew moshia'): the KJV's "saviour". The word comes from the root yasha', "to save, deliver", the root of the names Joshua, Isaiah and Jesus (Yeshua). In Judges and Kings it means someone God raises up to rescue His people from enemies.

13:6.t: "Asherah pole": the KJV's "grove". Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, and her symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree set up beside an altar. See 1 Kings 14:15.

13:7.t: "For Hazael had left": the KJV's "neither did he leave". The "he" is the king of Aram named at the end of the verse.

13:20.t: "Each spring": the KJV's "at the coming in of the year". The Hebrew new year began in spring, when armies went to war.

13:23.t: "Turned toward them": the KJV's "had respect unto them".

"Gracious", "compassion" (Hebrew hanan, racham): hanan is to show undeserved favor; racham, related to the word for womb, is the tender pity of a parent. Together they recall God's name in Exodus 34:6, "merciful and gracious".

14:7.t: "Sela": the KJV's "Selah", a rock fortress in Edom. Joktheel may mean "God destroys".

14:8.t: "Face each other in battle": the KJV's "look one another in the face", a challenge to fight.

14:11.t: "Face each other in battle": the KJV's "look one another in the face", a challenge to fight.

14:9.t: Jehoash's fable mocks Amaziah as a thistle asking a cedar for a marriage alliance.

14:12.t: "Every man fled home": the KJV's "fled every man to their tents", an old phrase for going home.

14:21.t: Azariah is also called Uzziah (15:13, 15:30-34; 2 Chronicles 26).

14:25.t: "Lebo-hamath": the KJV's "the entering in of Hamath", the northern limit of Israel (see 1 Kings 8:65). "The Sea of the Arabah": the KJV's "the sea of the plain", the Dead Sea. This Jonah is the prophet of the book of Jonah.

14:26.t: "No one left, slave or free": the KJV's "not any shut up, nor any left", a fixed phrase that probably means everyone, whether bound or free (see 9:8).

15:2.t: Jecoliah: the KJV spells it Jecholiah.

15:5.t: "A separate house": the KJV's "a several house". 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 tells why he was struck.

15:10.t: "In front of the people": some Greek manuscripts read "at Ibleam".

15:16.t: Tiphsah: some Greek manuscripts read Tappuah, a town nearer Tirzah.

15:19.t: Pul is the Babylonian throne name of Tiglath-pileser III (15:29). KJV: "a thousand talents of silver".

15:25.t: "Citadel": the KJV's "palace", the fortified part of the royal house. Argob and Arieh may have been killed with the king, or the words may name places.

15:29.t: Abel-beth-maacah: the KJV spells it Abel-beth-maachah.

15:30.t: "The twentieth year of Jotham": Jotham reigned sixteen years (15:33); the count runs on from his reign alongside his father, through the years of Ahaz.

16:3.t: "Pass through the fire": the KJV wording is kept. It means child sacrifice by burning, as 17:31 and Jeremiah 7:31 make plain.

17:17.t: "Pass through the fire": the KJV wording is kept. It means child sacrifice by burning, as 17:31 and Jeremiah 7:31 make plain.
"Divination and sorcery": the KJV's "divination and enchantments", seeking hidden knowledge by signs and casting spells (Deuteronomy 18:10).

21:6.t: "Pass through the fire": the KJV wording is kept. It means child sacrifice by burning, as 17:31 and Jeremiah 7:31 make plain.

"Fortune-telling and sorcery": the KJV's "observed times, and used enchantments". "Mediums and spiritists": the KJV's "familiar spirits and wizards", people who claimed to speak with the dead. Also 23:24.

16:6.t: "The people of Judah": the KJV's "the Jews", its first use in the Bible. Many Hebrew manuscripts and modern Bibles read "Edom" and "Edomites" for "Aram" and "Arameans" in this verse, since the two words differ by one letter in Hebrew.

16:10.t: "Model": the KJV's "fashion". 16:11 "Before": the KJV's "against", in the old sense of "in time for".

16:14.t: Ahaz moved Solomon's bronze altar aside and used his new Damascus-style altar, "the great altar", for the regular offerings.

16:17.t: "Side panels of the stands", "basins", "the Sea": the KJV's "borders of the bases", "laver" and "the sea", the temple furnishings described at 1 Kings 7:23-39.

16:18.t: "Covered way for the Sabbath": the KJV's "covert for the sabbath". Its purpose is not known; Ahaz removed it, and the king's private entrance, to please the king of Assyria.

17:3.t: "Tribute": the KJV's "presents", the yearly payment owed by a subject king.

17:4.t: So king of Egypt: perhaps an abbreviation of a city name (Sais) or of a pharaoh's name; he is not otherwise known.

17:9.t: "From watchtower to fortified city": the KJV's "from the tower of the watchmen to the fenced city", meaning everywhere, from the smallest outpost to the largest city. Also 18:8.

17:10.t: "Sacred pillars and Asherah poles": the KJV's "images and groves". Sacred pillars were standing stones set up for worship; Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, whose symbol was a wooden pole or carved tree. See 3:2 and 1 Kings 14:15.

17:14.t: "They were as stubborn": the KJV's "hardened their necks", like an ox that will not bend to the yoke.

17:16.t: "Cast metal images": the KJV's "molten images". "The host of heaven": the sun, moon and stars worshiped as gods.

17:24.t: Cuthah, Avva: the KJV spells them Cuthah and Ava, and Cuth in verse 30.

17:26.t: "The god of the land": lowercase, because the speakers are foreigners who think of the LORD as one local god among many.

17:29.t: "The people of Samaria": the KJV's "the Samaritans", here meaning the earlier Israelite inhabitants, not the later Samaritan community.

17:32.t: "All sorts of people": the KJV's "the lowest of them"; the Hebrew means from every part of their population, not only from the Levites. Compare 1 Kings 12:31.
They "feared the LORD" in that they added Him to their gods (17:33), but they did not fear Him as His covenant required (17:34-39).

18:2.t: Zechariah: the KJV spells it Zachariah.

18:4.t: "Nehushtan": the name sounds like the Hebrew words for "bronze" and "serpent". The KJV's "he called it" can also be read "it was called".

18:13.t: The Assyrian records of Sennacherib also tell of this campaign in 701 BC, his siege of the cities of Judah and the tribute paid by Hezekiah.

18:14.t: KJV: "three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold".

18:17.t: The Tartan, the Rabsaris and the Rab-shakeh: Assyrian titles, not personal names. Tartan means commander in chief; Rabsaris, chief officer; Rab-shakeh, chief cupbearer, a high official. "The Washerman's Field": the KJV's "the fuller's field", where cloth was washed and bleached.

18:18.t: "Secretary": the KJV's "scribe", a royal official. "Recorder": the keeper of royal records, perhaps also a herald.

18:21.t: "Broken reed": the KJV's "bruised reed", a cracked cane that splinters under weight.

18:23.t: "Make a bargain": the KJV's "give pledges", meaning a wager.

18:26.t: "Aramaic": the KJV's "the Syrian language", the language of diplomacy in that day. "The language of Judah": the KJV's "the Jews' language", Hebrew.

18:32.t: "Grain and new wine": the KJV's "corn and wine". In the KJV "corn" means grain of any kind.

18:34.t: Ivvah: the KJV spells it Ivah, here and at 19:13.

19:2.t: "The senior priests": the KJV's "the elders of the priests".

19:3.t: Children come to birth but the mother has no strength to deliver: a picture of a crisis with no way out.

19:9.t: "Cush": the KJV's "Ethiopia", its usual rendering of the Hebrew Cush, a land south of Egypt, as at Genesis 2:13. Tirhakah was a pharaoh of the Cushite dynasty that ruled Egypt.

19:12.t: Telassar: the KJV spells it Thelasar.

19:15.t: "Cherubim": the KJV's "cherubims". The Hebrew ending -im already makes the word plural.

19:21.t: A poem, given in prose lines here since each verse is one line. "The virgin daughter of Zion": Jerusalem pictured as a young woman.

19:23.t: "Pine trees": the KJV's "fir trees"; the exact tree is uncertain. "Its farthest lodging place, its finest forest": the KJV's "the lodgings of his borders, and into the forest of his Carmel".

19:24.t: "The places under siege": the KJV's "besieged places". The Hebrew word matsor can also be read as a name for Egypt, as many modern Bibles take it.

19:26.t: "Grain scorched before it grows up": the KJV's "corn blasted", struck by the hot east wind.

19:29.t: "This will be the sign for you, Hezekiah": the KJV's "unto thee"; Isaiah turns to address Hezekiah.

19:35.t: KJV: "an hundred fourscore and five thousand". "When the people got up": the KJV's "when they arose", meaning the Israelites or the surviving Assyrians.

19:37.t: Ararat: the KJV's "Armenia", the land of Urartu north of Assyria (compare Genesis 8:4). Esarhaddon: the KJV spells it Esar-haddon.

20:1.t: "Put your house in order": that is, make your final arrangements.

20:5.t: "Leader": the KJV's "captain", the Hebrew nagid, a ruler appointed by God.

20:7.t: "Cake of figs": the KJV's "lump of figs", a common poultice.

20:9.t: "Steps": the KJV's "degrees". The Hebrew word means steps, and "the dial of Ahaz" was probably a stairway whose steps marked the time by the shadow. "Stairway of Ahaz": the KJV's "dial of Ahaz".

20:12.t: Merodach-baladan: the KJV spells it Berodach-baladan, as in some Hebrew manuscripts; Isaiah 39:1 has Merodach.

20:13.t: "Welcomed": the KJV's "hearkened unto them"; some manuscripts read "rejoiced over them" (Isaiah 39:2).

20:19.t: "Peace and security": the KJV's "peace and truth". Hezekiah takes comfort that the disaster will not come in his lifetime.

20:20.t: "The tunnel": the KJV's "a conduit". This is probably Hezekiah's tunnel, cut through rock from the Gihon spring to the pool of Siloam, which can still be walked today.

21:1.t: Hephzibah: the name means "my delight is in her". The KJV spells it Hephzi-bah.

21:7.t: "The carved image of Asherah": the KJV's "a graven image of the grove".

21:12.t: "Will ring": the KJV's "both his ears shall tingle".

21:13.t: The measuring line and plumb line are builders' tools used here for tearing down: Jerusalem will be judged by the same standard as Samaria and the house of Ahab.

22:1.t: Bozkath: the KJV spells it Boscath.

22:8.t: "The Book of the Law": many think this was all or part of Deuteronomy, whose curses (Deuteronomy 28) would explain the king's alarm.

22:11.t: "The Book of the Law": many think this was all or part of Deuteronomy, whose curses (Deuteronomy 28) would explain the king's alarm.

22:9.t: "Emptied out": the KJV's "gathered", poured out from the chest.

22:12.t: Micaiah, Asaiah: the KJV spells them Michaiah and Asahiah.

22:14.t: "The Second Quarter": the KJV's "the college". The Hebrew mishneh means "second", a newer district of Jerusalem. "Keeper of the wardrobe": the robes of the king or of the priests.

22:20.t: "In peace": Josiah died in battle (23:29), but he was spared from seeing the fall of Jerusalem, which is the point of the promise.

23:3.t: "Committed themselves": the KJV's "stood to the covenant".

23:4.t: "Priests of the second rank": assistant priests under the high priest. "Fields of the Kidron": the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem.

23:5.t: "Idolatrous priests": the Hebrew kemarim, a word used only of priests of false gods. "Constellations": the KJV's "planets"; the Hebrew probably means the signs of the zodiac.

23:6.t: "The common people": the KJV's "the children of the people".

23:7.t: "Male shrine prostitutes": the KJV's "sodomites". The Hebrew qadesh, from the root for holiness, means men set apart for the service of a pagan shrine, where sexual rites were thought to be part of the worship. See 1 Kings 14:24. "Hangings": the Hebrew is literally "houses", perhaps tent shrines or garments for the goddess.

23:10.t: Topheth: a place in the Valley of Hinnom where children were burned. The name may come from a word for a fireplace. The Hebrew name of the valley, Ge-hinnom, became the New Testament word Gehenna.

23:11.t: "Official": the KJV's "chamberlain", the Hebrew saris, which can mean a eunuch or any court official. "Courtyard": the KJV's "suburbs"; the Hebrew parvarim probably names a colonnade or court on the west of the temple.

23:13.t: "East of Jerusalem, to the south of the Mount of Corruption": the KJV's "before Jerusalem, which were on the right hand of the mount of corruption". "Before" means east, and "right hand" means south, for a person facing east. The Mount of Corruption is the southern part of the Mount of Olives, named for the idols there (1 Kings 11:7).
"Detestable goddess", "detestable god": the KJV's "abomination", a word used of idols.

23:16.t: This fulfills the prophecy of the man of God from Judah, spoken some 300 years earlier (1 Kings 13:1-2, 13:31-32).

23:17.t: "Monument": the KJV's "title", a marker over a grave.

23:24.t: "Household idols": the KJV's "images", the Hebrew teraphim, small household idols (see Genesis 31:19).

23:29.t: Pharaoh Neco: the KJV's "Pharaoh-nechoh". "Went up against the king of Assyria": the KJV's reading. Records from Babylon show that Neco went north to help Assyria against Babylon in 609 BC, so most modern Bibles read "to"; the Hebrew al can mean either. "As soon as he saw him": the KJV's "when he had seen him", meaning when they met.

23:33.t: KJV: "an hundred talents of silver, and a talent of gold".

23:35.t: "Assessment": the KJV's "taxation", the amount assessed on each person.

24:2.t: Chaldeans: the KJV's "Chaldees", the people of southern Babylonia, who ruled Babylon in this period.

24:7.t: "The Brook of Egypt": the KJV's "the river of Egypt", a stream bed at the southwest border, not the Nile. See 1 Kings 8:65.

24:12.t: "In the eighth year of his reign": the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, 597 BC.

24:14.t: "Metalworkers": the KJV's "smiths". The numbers in 24:14 and 24:16 seem to count the same exiles in different ways.

24:16.t: "Metalworkers": the KJV's "smiths". The numbers in 24:14 and 24:16 seem to count the same exiles in different ways.

24:17.t: "Jehoiachin's uncle": the KJV's "his father's brother". Mattaniah was another son of Josiah.

25:1.t: "Siege works": the KJV's "forts", towers or walls built around a besieged city.

25:3.t: "The fourth month": as in Jeremiah 52:6. The KJV supplies "of the fourth month", which the Hebrew of this verse leaves out.

25:4.t: "The Arabah": the KJV's "the plain", the Jordan valley.

25:7.t: "Bronze chains": the KJV's "fetters of brass"; "brass" in 1611 meant copper or bronze (see Genesis 4:22).

25:8.t: Nebuzaradan: the KJV spells it Nebuzar-adan.

25:12.t: "To work the vineyards and the fields": the KJV's "vinedressers and husbandmen".

25:14.t: "Dishes": the KJV's "spoons", here small pans for incense.

25:17.t: KJV: "eighteen cubits" and "three cubits". "Capital": the KJV's "chapiter", the top of a pillar. 1 Kings 7:16 gives the capitals as five cubits; the three here may leave out a decorated section.

25:19.t: "The king's council": the KJV's "them that were in the king's presence", his close advisers. KJV: "threescore men".

25:23.t: Kareah: the KJV spells it Careah. "The son of the Maacathite": the KJV's "the son of a Maachathite".

25:25.t: "The people of Judah": the KJV's "the Jews".

25:27.t: "Released": the KJV's "did lift up the head of", an idiom for showing favor. Evil-merodach (Babylonian Amel-Marduk, "man of Marduk") reigned 562-560 BC. The name has nothing to do with the English word "evil".

25:28.t: "Gave him a seat of honor": the KJV's "set his throne above the throne of the kings". The book ends with the line of David still alive in exile.

1:3.t: "The angel of the LORD" (Hebrew malakh YHWH): malakh means messenger, human or heavenly. "The angel of the LORD" sometimes speaks as God Himself (Genesis 16:10-13, Exodus 3:2-6), and interpreters differ on whether he is a created angel or an appearance of God. We keep "angel", lowercase, as the KJV has it. See 1 Kings 19:7.

1:15.t: "The angel of the LORD" (Hebrew malakh YHWH): malakh means messenger, human or heavenly. "The angel of the LORD" sometimes speaks as God Himself (Genesis 16:10-13, Exodus 3:2-6), and interpreters differ on whether he is a created angel or an appearance of God. We keep "angel", lowercase, as the KJV has it. See 1 Kings 19:7.

2:9.t: "A double share" (Hebrew pi shenayim, "a mouth of two"): the same phrase gives the firstborn son a double portion of his father's estate (Deuteronomy 21:17). Elisha is not asking to be twice as great as Elijah, but to be his true heir and successor, as the sons of the prophets recognize in 2:15.

2:11.t: "Whirlwind" (Hebrew se'arah): a storm wind or tempest, the same word used when God answers Job "out of the whirlwind" (Job 38:1). It is a storm sign of God's presence, not necessarily a tornado.

3:27.t: "Great fury against Israel" (Hebrew qetsef gadol): qetsef usually means divine wrath, but the text does not say whose. It may be the LORD's anger, the fury of the Moabites, or the horror and dismay of Israel at the sacrifice. The KJV's "great indignation" leaves it open, and so do we.

5:1.t: "Leprosy" (Hebrew tsara'at): a name for many skin diseases, and even for mold on cloth and walls (Leviticus 13-14), not only Hansen's disease. It made a person ritually unclean. "Leprosy" is kept as the familiar word.

5:27.t: "Leprosy" (Hebrew tsara'at): a name for many skin diseases, and even for mold on cloth and walls (Leviticus 13-14), not only Hansen's disease. It made a person ritually unclean. "Leprosy" is kept as the familiar word.

5:10.t: "Clean" (Hebrew tahar): ritually pure, fit to take part in worship and community life, not only physically washed. Naaman is cured of a disease and also made acceptable before God.

5:14.t: "Clean" (Hebrew tahar): ritually pure, fit to take part in worship and community life, not only physically washed. Naaman is cured of a disease and also made acceptable before God.

5:18.t: Rimmon: the storm god of Damascus, also called Hadad. The name sounds like the Hebrew for "pomegranate", and the Hebrew writers may have spelled it to mock him, from ram ("thunderer").

9:22.t: "Prostitution" (Hebrew zenunim): the KJV's "whoredoms". Throughout the prophets this word describes unfaithfulness to the LORD by worshiping other gods, as a wife unfaithful to her husband. "Sorceries" (keshaphim) are magic arts forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10.

13:17.t: "Victory" (Hebrew teshu'ah): the KJV's "deliverance", from the same root as "deliverer" in 13:5. The arrow is a sign that the LORD Himself gives the victory.

17:15.t: "Worthless idols", "became worthless" (Hebrew hevel): the KJV's "vanity". Hevel means breath or vapor, something that has no substance; it is the word behind "vanity of vanities" in Ecclesiastes (see 1 Kings 16:13). The Hebrew plays on the word: they went after hevel and became hevel, as empty as the gods they followed.

18:5.t: "Trusted" (Hebrew batach): to rely on, to feel secure in. The verb runs through chapters 18-19 like a refrain: the Rab-shakeh asks what Hezekiah trusts in (18:19-24, 18:30) and Sennacherib warns him not to let his God deceive him (19:10). The story answers that the LORD alone is worth trusting.

18:6.t: "Held fast" (Hebrew davaq): the KJV's "clave". It is the verb used when a man "clings" to his wife (Genesis 2:24), and in Deuteronomy for Israel holding fast to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20).

19:4.t: "The living God" (Hebrew elohim chay): the title contrasts the LORD with the idols of wood and stone that the Assyrians had burned (19:18). The Assyrian king's insult is aimed not at a city but at the God who lives and acts.

19:16.t: "The living God" (Hebrew elohim chay): the title contrasts the LORD with the idols of wood and stone that the Assyrians had burned (19:18). The Assyrian king's insult is aimed not at a city but at the God who lives and acts.

19:7.t: "Put a spirit in him" (Hebrew ruach): the KJV's "send a blast upon him". See Genesis 1:2: ruach means spirit, wind or breath. Here it probably means God will move Sennacherib's mind or will, so that a report sends him home.

19:22.t: "The Holy One of Israel" (Hebrew qedosh Yisra'el): a favorite title of Isaiah, used about 25 times in his book and rarely elsewhere. "Holy" (qadosh) means set apart, wholly other, and morally pure. The title joins God's otherness to His closeness: the Holy One belongs to Israel.

19:30.t: "Remnant" (Hebrew she'erit) and "survivors" (peletah): those who are left after judgment. The idea runs through Isaiah and the later prophets: God judges His people but keeps a remnant through whom His promises go on.

19:31.t: "The zeal of the LORD" (Hebrew qin'ah): the KJV's "zeal". The word means burning devotion that will not share a loved one with a rival, and is also translated "jealousy" (see 1 Kings 19:10). Here it is God's fierce devotion to His people.

21:2.t: "Detestable practices" (Hebrew to'evah): the KJV's "abominations". The word means something abhorrent, especially to God, and is used of idol worship and the practices that went with it, such as child sacrifice and sorcery.

21:11.t: "Detestable practices" (Hebrew to'evah): the KJV's "abominations". The word means something abhorrent, especially to God, and is used of idol worship and the practices that went with it, such as child sacrifice and sorcery.

22:13.t: "Wrath" (Hebrew chemah): heat, burning anger. The image of fire is kept in "burns against us" and "will not be put out". It is not a sudden temper but God's settled opposition to evil, here provoked by long unfaithfulness.

22:17.t: "Wrath" (Hebrew chemah): heat, burning anger. The image of fire is kept in "burns against us" and "will not be put out". It is not a sudden temper but God's settled opposition to evil, here provoked by long unfaithfulness.

22:19.t: "Your heart was tender" (Hebrew rakh levavkha): the heart in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will more than of feeling (see 1 Kings 3:9). Josiah's was soft and responsive, not hardened. He stands in contrast to the people who "hardened their necks" (17:14).

23:25.t: "With all his heart, all his soul and all his strength" (Hebrew lev, nephesh, me'od): the words of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:5), and Josiah is the only king said to have fulfilled them. The heart (lev) is the seat of thought and will; nephesh is the whole living self, a living, breathing person (see Genesis 2:7); me'od means "very much", so "with all his muchness", all he had.
